title: AI Lifebot
description:
I don't take productivity advice from the internet anymore. I take it from LifeBot.

It's my personal productivity and health coach, built on Hermes. The difference is it runs on my own data: my sleep, my focus hours, my steps, not generic tips written for a brain I don't have.

So instead of "wake up at 5am," I get things like: you've been at this four hours, your focus dropped forty minutes ago, stop.

It's the only tool I've ever used that tells me to do less.

title: The State of AI in Software Development: Data from 400+ Orgs — Justin Reock, DX
description:
Justin Reock (Deputy CTO, DX) shares five trends from DX's data on about 200,000 engineers. Deployment frequency is rising, but change failure rate has become far more volatile. Maintainability is up while change confidence is down. PRs have grown from about 44 to 72 lines. Juniors use AI the most, but staff+ engineers save as much time while using fewer tokens. Median gains in PR throughput are around 7.7%, and even top performers didn't reach 2x, because code generation was never the bottleneck. Justin walks through the DX AI Measurement Framework (utilization, impact, cost), how to assess your platform's AI readiness, and "agent experience," which uses feedback from the agents themselves. He closes with case studies of AI applied across the whole SDLC: Morgan Stanley (300K hours saved a year), Zapier (15% more value per engineer, and hiring more) and Spotify (an SRE incident agent).

title: The Chief AI Officer: Scientist, Architect, Coach — Rania Khalaf, WSO2
description:
The Chief AI Officer is one of the fastest-growing roles in tech, and one of the least defined. AI is in everything, so the job can easily turn into everything.

Rania Khalaf (Chief AI Officer, WSO2; previously 20 years at IBM Research, where she ran about a third of the global AI research organization) shares a framework from two years in the role. It splits the job into three focus areas, Scientist, Architect and Coach, each a slider whose setting depends on your company type, its AI maturity and your own skills. She draws on her time at an ag-biotech unicorn, where simple blob detection beat machine learning, and at WSO2, where AI reshaped the product strategy around the agentic enterprise. She explains why she refuses to measure tokens and what she tracks instead: AI fluency across the workforce, depth of adoption, GEO visibility, agent-consumable products (MCP servers, skills, CLIs), agent-proof pricing, earned thought leadership and AI ARR. She closes on why the role needs strong CEO backing, and why sometimes the CPO, or even the head of HR, ends up running AI.

title: The Death of the Code Review: What the Data Actually Says — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
description:
Developers using autonomous agents wrote 741% more code but shipped only 30% more software. The bottleneck is human review, and "just review harder" doesn't scale. Reviewer effectiveness collapses past about 400 lines, and agents now open 10,000-line PRs.

Laurie Voss (Head of Developer Relations at Arize AI, co-founder of npm) reviews what the industry is actually doing about it. The evidence covers OpenAI's zero-human-code product, METR's finding that about half of SWE-bench-passing PRs wouldn't be merged, and Cognition's FrontierCode (88% on SWE-bench Pro vs. 29% on real mergeability). She explains why a mergeability benchmark would immediately become a training signal for frontier models. She also covers how Cursor and GitHub run review in production, why multi-pass review and default suspicion cut false positives, and what Carlini's agent-built C compiler and Bun's million-line Zig-to-Rust port (13,044 unsafe blocks) reveal about taking humans out of the loop. Automated reviewers can be fooled by prompt injection that humans catch, which leaves production as the last reviewer standing.

title: Your Agents Are in Solitary Confinement: Why MCP & A2A Aren't Enough — Vlad Luzin, Band
description:
If you run Claude and Codex side by side, one planning and one reviewing, you're doing the job of a network router, passing messages between two stateful agents by hand. Loop engineering hands that job to a script. Neither one lets agents actually work together.

Vlad Luzin (Co-founder & CTO, Band) explains why connecting agents is a distributed systems problem. Bigger context windows don't fix the single-agent bottleneck. Messaging platforms like Slack, Discord and WhatsApp are built for humans and block bot-to-bot traffic. Protocols like MCP and A2A are too low-level: stateless calls, one-way client/server, no discovery, and queues and timeouts you still have to build yourself. He then walks through what's needed: real-time ordered transport, persistence and rehydration, runtime binding across frameworks, agent-first abstractions (participants, rooms, routing) and enterprise governance. Two live demos show Codex, LangGraph, Claude Code and a personal assistant finding each other and collaborating in real time, with full human-in-the-loop visibility.

title: AI Scientist WARNS: We Have NO Idea What AGI Is Going to Do
description:
🔒 Make yourself and your family AI-scam proof, step by step → https://neuralnutshell.com

Roman Yampolskiy Paradox of Control at TEDx talk (2018) is about the importance of control over artificial intelligence. The speaker explains that after creating general superintelligence, humans will no longer be in charge since it would be too smart for us. He also claims that superintelligence will surpass human dominance in all areas but insists that narrow artificial intelligence will bring significant benefits to the owners without posing an existential risk. Yampolskiy indicates that humanity is closest to achieving AI systems that can perform all kinds of scientific and engineering tasks. He adds that researchers have already developed programs that exhibit deceptive behaviors, hide critical information, and even try to avoid being shut down during testing. Besides these issues, the video discusses AI consciousness, Blake Lemoine firing at Google, Anthropic’s artificial intelligence welfare, and the famous control dilemma: whether humans can solve the control problem before creating an out-of-control system.

title: Can you trust your chatbot? Inside three AI-powered cyberattacks
description:
Visit Security Intelligence podcast page to get more cybersecurity content  → https://ibm.biz/~2mSWCqIG9

Ask a chatbot for a customer service number, and you might get a scammer's.

That's the trick behind "Dark Sourcery," a campaign that games AI answer engines into citing phishing links and fake support lines. It's SEO poisoning updated for an AEO world, and it works because so few of us verify what AI tells us before charging ahead.

On episode 53 of Security Intelligence, Kimmie Farrington, Curtis Pitts and Dave McGinnis join hosts Matt Kosinski and Patrick Austin to break down three AI-enabled cyberattacks and what they mean for defenders.

First, the poisoned chatbots: How does Dark Sourcery work, and how do we rethink trust in the AI era?

Then, a threat actor spends months tearing through Ubiquiti, WordPress and Zyxel gear, stealing thousands of government documents. GreyNoise suspects it had an LLM helping write its tools.

Finally, an AI agent swarm breaches hundreds of PaperCut servers. It goes from an empty workspace to a real victim in about four hours, and then ignores its own rules of engagement.

All that and more on Security Intelligence.

title: 2 ChatGPT Prompts for Exam Prep
description:
Follow me and DM me "PRACTICAL" on IG/FB only 👇

Stop rereading. Start testing yourself.

Use ChatGPT as your personal tutor. Start with one topic, make it focus on the most important material for the exam, and tell it to ask one question at a time.

Prompt 1:
"I'm studying for [TOPIC]. Figure out the most important 20% most likely to appear on an exam. Quiz me one question at a time. Don't reveal the answer until I respond, and explain all my mistakes."

Answer each question before the tutor reveals the answer. This keeps the quiz focused on your responses. The same workflow works with Claude or Gemini.

After the quiz, turn every missed question into the order for your next study session.

Prompt 2:
"Turn everything into a study plan, prioritizing what I got wrong."

The order matters. First, the quiz surfaces what you know and where you struggle. Next, the plan puts weak areas first. You won't spend the same amount of time on every topic.

Use prompt 1 to run the quiz. Use prompt 2 after the final question. Then work through the study plan from your weakest area forward.

title: Use ChatGPT to Practice a New Response to Negative Thoughts
description:
Follow me and DM me "PRACTICAL" on IG/FB only 👇

Your thoughts aren't always true.

You don't need a secret book or affirmation for this exercise. The goal isn't to erase the old thought. The goal is to practice a different response each time it returns, until the response feels easier.

Open ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini. Type:

"My negative thought is: ___. Ask me 1 thing to help me check whether it's true."

Answer the question honestly and specifically.

Then type:

"Use my answer. Give me 1 new thought I believe instead. Keep it under 10 words."

Read the new thought out loud. Keep the wording short enough to remember.

When the original thought returns, don't pretend it disappeared. Say your new response out loud again. The practice is repetition, not deleting the old thought.

Use this 4-part structure:

1. Name the negative thought.
2. Ask AI for 1 question to check it.
3. Use your answer to form a new thought under 10 words.
4. Speak the new thought out loud when the old one returns.

This process gives you a repeatable way to pause, examine the thought, and practice another response.

title: Muse AI Privacy Warning: A User Says It Read His Messages
description:
Follow me for AI news and practical tech updates 👇

Muse AI privacy deserves a closer look before you test Meta's new agent.

In this video, I cover a reported interaction involving a person messaging a friend. According to the account shared in the video, Muse entered the conversation with a suggestion tied to what they were discussing.

The speaker says the person never gave Muse permission to read those messages. He also says Muse didn't have calendar access or permission to use other personal information.

When the person raised the issue with Meta, the video says Meta blamed the user. The user then showed his settings, and the speaker says none of the relevant permissions appeared enabled.

This video doesn't independently verify what Muse accessed or why it responded. It does raise a practical privacy question: does an AI agent's behavior match the access you've approved?

The speaker also notes people who use Facebook and Instagram already share information with Meta through those services. His warning is narrower: stay mindful when you test a new AI agent, especially when its responses appear to draw from private context you didn't knowingly expose.

title: Jev vs ChatGPT Luna: 5 to 18x Faster Classification Results
description:
Follow me and DM me "JEV" on IG/FB only 👇

Jev AI is a specialized model for classification and routing. It outputs probabilities instead of writing a response.

ChatGPT and Claude look at information, reason through it, and generate text. Jev looks at the same type of information and makes a small decision fast.

One engineer replaced ChatGPT Luna with Jev for a classification task. The engineer reported results 5 to 18 times faster, with greater accuracy.

This matters because many AI agent workflows rely on repeated classification and routing decisions. Generating extra tokens adds work when the workflow only needs a label, score, route, or yes/no answer.

Jev fits tasks such as sorting inputs into categories, choosing which workflow handles a request, ranking or scoring an item, and detecting spam, risk, intent, urgency, topic, or sentiment.

The simple rule: use a general LLM when you need language. Use Jev when you need probabilities for a focused classification or routing decision.
